prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity into trade theory, showing how selection, reallocation and exporting decisions shape the gains from trade

statement.case_for: The heterogeneous-firm framework changed the unit of analysis in international trade from the industry to the firm. It brought selection into exporting, within-industry reallocation and productivity-driven gains into a tractable general-equilibrium model, and it moved the empirical agenda toward firm-level microdata. It has had more than two decades to be confirmed across many countries and datasets, and it is now canonical in teaching and policy analysis. Attribution is cleaner than in most shortlisted candidates. Melitz (2003) is the originating model, and Helpman, through Helpman–Melitz–Yeaple on exports versus foreign direct investment and his wider firm-level trade work, is the natural co-recipient. The 2008 prize covered earlier new trade theory, and this work is a distinct later advance rather than a repeat. I judge this on method, scope and durability, as I would for any field. Among the shortlisted candidates it combines a clear conceptual break, long confirmation and a credit boundary that can be drawn with reasonable confidence.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related early empirical and theoretical contributions that this ballot does not credit, and Redding's quantitative extensions are also left out. A two-person award would therefore draw a boundary that parts of the field would contest. Trade was recognised in 2008, which may reduce appetite for a second trade prize. The quantitative welfare magnitudes depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity draws and CES demand. B038 has broader support and speaks directly to current debates on technology and globalisation, so it is a serious rival.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B038 first because the task-based and China-shock strands are separable, well documented and empirically credible. He ranks B044 second, noting that it builds on Krugman's 2008 prize rather than duplicating it, and that Redding's strongest links are to later quantitative spatial work.
responses.response: I agree on the Krugman point and on Redding's later role. I also rate B038 highly, as my second rank shows. Where I differ is attribution. Boppart himself notes that the task framework owes much to Acemoglu, who is not credited here and was recognised in 2024. The China-shock strand also requires dropping Dorn from the three-person cap. B038 is therefore an important body of work whose credit boundary is blurred by neighbouring prizes and by two distinct strands. B044 has a more singular originating contribution. If the Committee wants a labour-and-technology prize, I would want the argument made on which strand carries the discovery, not on combining them.

responses.point: Andersson ranks law and finance (B003) first for its durable empirical agenda across finance, comparative law and development. He concedes that the legal-origins thesis has been challenged on causal identification and variable coding, and that choosing among four co-authors is a judgement call.
responses.response: I take the breadth of influence seriously. But the reservations he lists weigh heavily for me. As an economic historian, I find the legal-origins coding and the treatment of colonial history the weakest part of the empirical case, and omitting Vishny leaves a legitimate claimant out. By comparison, firm-heterogeneity trade theory has been tested against firm-level data in many countries without its core predictions being overturned. Its disputes concern welfare magnitudes, not whether the mechanism exists. I therefore do not rank B003 above B044. I would want a clearer account of whether the identification critiques have been answered before supporting it.

responses.point: Krusell ranks political economics (B017) first as a coherent, rigorous field linking constitutions, electoral rules, state capacity and fiscal policy. He acknowledges possible overlap with the 2024 institutions prize and that some causal claims rest on cross-country identification.
responses.response: The credited trio is well delimited, and I ranked B017 sixth because I accept that it created a field. His own caveats are my reasons for placing it below B044. Cross-country constitutional comparisons have limited identification, and the proximity to the 2024 prize reduces the incremental case. I would not treat the overlap as disqualifying, but I do not think it has a stronger case on scientific durability or sharpness of attribution than B044. I keep B017 outside my alternatives for that reason.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would treat Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as co-equal originators of the firm-heterogeneity agenda, which would make a two-person boundary hard to defend.
Whether Redding's quantitative spatial and trade contribution should be credited alongside Melitz and Helpman, or is better recognised separately later.
How much weight to give the 2008 trade prize and the 2024 institutions prize when judging thematic balance.
Whether the dependence of gains-from-trade magnitudes on functional-form assumptions is a serious weakness or an ordinary limit of structural work.
Whether B038 should be preferred because of its broader relevance, if its credit boundary relative to Acemoglu and the choice between Hanson and Dorn can be resolved.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. I am an economic historian at Lund, and none of the credited names for B044 appears among my documented co-authors or institutional connections. Lund colleagues and cross-disciplinary collaborations with political scientists are documented, but they do not relate to the B044 credited names.
